# Land Tenure Arrangements in Ghana

Between 2012/13 and 2016/17 Ghanaian land tenure moved on two margins at once, and both moved the same way. Fewer farmers owned the land they cultivated, and those who did own held a thinner bundle of rights over it. Ownership became not only less common but less consequential, in the sense that the entitlements which make it economically useful, the capacity to pledge land as collateral or to transfer it, were exercised by a shrinking minority. What expanded in its place were the flexible, socially mediated arrangements customary systems supply: allocation by family or village, use free of charge, and above all sharecropping. This section traces that movement in aggregate (Table 2) and then across production systems (Tables S1--S4), because it fixes the institutional conditions under which the productivity comparisons that follow are made. If the entitlements ownership confers carry the productive advantage conventionally attributed to them, a period in which those entitlements are in retreat is where that advantage should be easiest to detect.

At the aggregate level, the share of farmers operating on land they do not own rose from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Not owned","c1")` percent in 2012/13 to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Not owned","c2")` percent in 2016/17, while ownership without formal documentation declined from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Owned without documentation","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Owned without documentation","c2")` percent. Ownership with formal documentation increased only modestly, from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Owned with documentation","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Owned with documentation","c2")` percent. Reported ownership therefore contracted overall, and the modest growth in documented holdings did not offset the decline in undocumented ownership or the expansion of non-ownership arrangements.

This divergence becomes even more apparent when ownership rights are considered. Over the same period, the proportion of farmers reporting no ownership rights increased from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","No rights","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","No rights","c2")` percent, pointing to a widening gap between nominal ownership and effective control over land. At the same time, access to key economic rights weakened. The share of farmers able to use land as collateral fell from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c2")` percent, while those able to sell land declined from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be sold","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be sold","c2")` percent. Similarly, the proportion of farmers holding both sale and collateral rights dropped from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c2")` percent. The two movements therefore compound rather than offset one another: fewer farmers reported owning land, and among those who did, a shrinking share could exercise the rights that matter for long-term investment, access to finance, and land-based decision-making.

The increase in land tenure insecurity can be linked to a combination of institutional and structural factors within Ghana's land sector. Although reforms such as the Land Administration Project (Phase II, 2011--2018) were intended to improve land registration systems and strengthen tenure security, their implementation remained uneven, especially in rural areas where customary land systems still dominate [@Ghebru2017; @Barnes2026; @Mwamba2024]. As a result, many farmers continued to operate without formal documentation, limiting their ability to transfer land or use it as collateral [@Ghebru2017; @Barnes2026]. In addition, rising population pressure, land fragmentation, and the expansion of commercial agriculture intensified competition for land and increased reliance on informal arrangements such as family allocation, borrowing, and sharecropping [@Ubink2007; @Aslam2025; @Dhakal2025; @Obayelu2017]. Weak rural credit markets further reduced the economic value of land ownership, since customary holdings are rarely accepted as collateral.

These institutional features matter for how the ownership categories recorded in Table 2 should be read, because in Ghana effective security has been shown to rest on something other than paper. Working in Akwapim, @Goldstein2008 find that individuals holding powerful positions in the local political hierarchy enjoy more secure rights over the plots those positions govern, invest more in land fertility as a result, and obtain substantially higher output. The relationship holds plot by plot within a single cultivator, which is what makes it informative: security varies with the political standing that attaches to a given parcel rather than with any attribute of the farmer. On that account, documentation and social position are alternative routes to the same protection, and a farmer well placed in the customary hierarchy may be as secure without a deed as another farmer is with one. A survey instrument that records documentation therefore measures only one of the two, and the ownership categories used throughout this paper should be understood accordingly.

Land acquisition patterns reinforce this broader picture. A majority of farmers accessed land through family or village allocation, although this declined only slightly from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Distributed by village/family","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Distributed by village/family","c2")` percent, indicating the continued dominance of customary systems. Access to land free of charge declined from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Use free of charge","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Use free of charge","c2")` percent, although such informal, socially mediated access remains sizeable. Sharecropping arrangements also increased from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Sharecropping","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Sharecropping","c2")` percent, indicating a growing dependence on flexible but potentially less secure forms of land access. Although rental markets remained relatively small, they changed only modestly, while land purchases declined from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Purchased","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","Purchased","c2")` percent, suggesting that formal land market transactions remain limited.

The distribution of sharecropping intensity points in the same direction. The proportion of farmers not engaged in sharecropping declined from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","0","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","0","c2")` percent, while the share under moderate-intensity arrangements (1-49 percent of land) rose from `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","1-49","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","1-49","c2")` percent and high-intensity arrangements (50-100 percent) held roughly steady (`r tbl_pct("table2.csv","50-100","c1")` percent to `r tbl_pct("table2.csv","50-100","c2")` percent). Although most farmers still operate outside sharecropping systems, a growing minority depend on such arrangements for land access. In this sense, land access is becoming more flexible, but not necessarily more secure.

The crop-level results (Tables S1--S4) show how these changes play out across different production systems. Ownership status by crop (Table S1) shows that informal ownership, particularly ownership without formal documentation, remains widespread among staple crop producers. It is especially high among beans (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Beans","c2")` percent), sorghum (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Sorghum","c2")` percent), millet (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Millet","c2")` percent), and rice (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Rice","c2")` percent), suggesting that farmers engaged in subsistence-oriented production are among the most exposed to insecure ownership conditions. Studying Ghana's rice industry directly, @Donkor2014 report that tenure arrangements bear on resource-use productivity and efficiency in exactly this segment, which places the descriptive pattern here alongside evidence that it carries production consequences. By comparison, crops associated with higher market value and longer-term investment, such as cocoa (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Cocoa","c3")` percent), banana (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Banana","c3")` percent), and plantain (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Plantain","c3")` percent), show relatively higher levels of documented ownership. This likely reflects the greater need for stronger tenure security in perennial and commercially oriented production systems, where investment periods are longer and returns depend on sustained control over land.

A similar pattern is observed when examining non-ownership across crop groups. Farming on land not owned by the household is particularly common among producers of banana (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Banana","c1")` percent), cocoyam (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Cocoyam","c1")` percent), and cassava (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Cassava","c1")` percent), indicating a greater reliance on borrowed, rented, or sharecropped land for these crops. In contrast, cereals such as sorghum (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Sorghum","c1")` percent) and millet (`r tbl_pct("tableS1.csv","Millet","c1")` percent) show lower levels of non-ownership, suggesting more direct control over land in the areas where these crops dominate. These differences likely reflect both agroecological conditions and the continued influence of customary inheritance systems in shaping land distribution.

The mode of land acquisition (Table S2) also varies considerably across crops. Overall, `r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","All crops listed","c1")` percent of farmers accessed land through family or village distribution, but this share rises to `r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Millet","c1")` percent for millet, `r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Sorghum","c1")` percent for sorghum, and `r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Rice","c1")` percent for rice, indicating the importance of communal allocation in staple production systems. Access to land free of charge is especially common among peanuts (`r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Peanut","c2")` percent) and yam (`r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Yam","c2")` percent), again pointing to the importance of informal and temporary arrangements. Sharecropping is more prevalent among banana (`r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Banana","c3")` percent), cocoa (`r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Cocoa","c3")` percent), and palm (`r tbl_pct("tableS2.csv","Palm","c3")` percent) producers, suggesting that such arrangements are particularly useful in crop systems that require higher labour and capital inputs. Although still less common overall, rental and purchase arrangements are relatively more visible among producers of tomato, eggplant, and cocoa, indicating a gradual movement toward more market-based land access in parts of the agricultural sector.

The crop-specific distribution of ownership rights (Table S3) provides further evidence of uneven tenure security. Large proportions of millet (`r tbl_pct("tableS3.csv","Millet","c1")` percent), sorghum (`r tbl_pct("tableS3.csv","Sorghum","c1")` percent), and beans (`r tbl_pct("tableS3.csv","Beans","c1")` percent) producers report having no formal ownership rights, and only very small shares can use land as collateral or sell it. This points to weak enforceability of rights in staple crop systems. By comparison, producers of cocoa (`r tbl_pct("tableS3.csv","Cocoa","c4")` percent) and palm (`r tbl_pct("tableS3.csv","Palm","c4")` percent) exhibit relatively stronger ownership security, with greater access to transfer and collateral rights. This suggests that secure and transferable land rights remain concentrated among farmers engaged in higher-value, commercially oriented, and longer-term agricultural production.

The role of sharecropping (Table S4) also varies substantially across crops. While the majority of farmers overall (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","All crops listed","c1")` percent) cultivate land outside sharecropping systems, high-intensity sharecropping is particularly common among banana (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Banana","c3")` percent), cocoyam (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Cocoyam","c3")` percent), and palm (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Palm","c3")` percent) producers. In these cases, sharecropping appears to serve as an important mechanism for facilitating access to land in crop systems that require more labour and capital. Evidence from Ghanaian cocoa supports that reading and refines it: @Donkor2023 find that tenure arrangements act unevenly across inputs, with family land title bearing more on fertiliser and land investment while sharecropping bears more on the adoption of hybrid seedlings. Tenure form therefore shapes not only how much farmers invest but which margin they invest on, which is one reason a single ownership contrast can conceal offsetting effects. By contrast, staple crops such as millet (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Millet","c1")` percent non-sharecropped), sorghum (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Sorghum","c1")` percent), and peanuts (`r tbl_pct("tableS4.csv","Peanut","c1")` percent) show very limited reliance on sharecropping, reflecting stronger dependence on direct or customary land access.

Overall, the combined evidence from Table 2 and Tables S1--S4 points to a land ownership system in transition. Reported ownership is contracting, effective ownership rights are weakening, and informal, flexible, and often less secure access arrangements are becoming increasingly important. At the same time, strong and transferable land rights remain concentrated among farmers engaged in higher-value and longer-term crop production. This dual structure highlights persistent inequalities in land access and ownership security, with important implications for agricultural investment, productivity, and rural development. Whether such changes register in production is a separate question, and the West African evidence counsels caution in answering it: pooling nine datasets from the region, @Fenske2011 finds the tenure-investment link significant for fallow and tree planting but not across investments generally, and finds that whether a study detects a link depends appreciably on its sample size, its measure of investment, and whether it controls for household fixed effects. The sections that follow therefore treat the institutional shift documented here as a question to be tested rather than a result to be assumed.
